Several apparently pure foodservice equipment repair/parts distributors, including restaurant facilities maintenance and OEM replacement-parts networks, appear private or embedded inside larger distributors; later layers should search private comparables to identify public suppliers to those networks.
MIDD is the cleanest public reference name for commercial restaurant kitchen equipment and parts exposure, but it is not a hidden small-cap discovery.

WEST should be tracked as an underfollowed beverage-platform infrastructure candidate because its filings disclose restaurant/foodservice customers and company-owned beverage equipment deployed at customer sites.

FARM is a high-risk micro-cap exception with unusually direct evidence for restaurant coffee equipment servicing; it requires liquidity, balance-sheet, and customer-retention verification before surviving later layers.

Restaurant beverage programs create a recurring equipment-plus-consumables loop: installed machines or customer beverage equipment may pull through coffee, tea, extract, syrup, maintenance, and service revenue.

The purest restaurant equipment service networks and parts distributors appear largely private, so public-market mapping may require adjacent exposures such as B2B coffee suppliers, refrigeration OEMs, diversified equipment makers, and aftermarket parts disclosures.
MIDD should remain the reference anchor for restaurant commercial kitchen, beverage, refrigeration, ice, oven, fryer, and connected-equipment exposure, but it is not the main underfollowed target.

FARM is the most node-specific speculative shadow candidate found for recurring restaurant beverage equipment service and DSD route density, but micro-cap liquidity, profitability, and balance-sheet risk require early disqualification checks.

WEST belongs in the underfollowed beverage supply-chain lane for restaurants and foodservice, but its role is more ingredient/formulation/supply-chain than equipment maintenance unless filings show dispenser or equipment-service obligations.

Many pure restaurant equipment service networks and parts distributors appear private, including technician-service and replacement-parts specialists; public-market mapping may require adjacent distributors, appliance OEMs, beverage suppliers, or facility-service proxies.

For later Serenity layers, prioritize proof of recurring service revenue, installed base, technician density, replacement-parts revenue, beverage-machine uptime obligations, and franchise/chain customer relationships over generic restaurant exposure.

node: Restaurant equipment, beverage machines, service, and maintenance networks
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Expanded the direct public-company universe for restaurant equipment, beverage platforms, and service/maintenance networks. The cleanest reference exposures are Middleby and ITW Food Equipment Group because they manufacture and service broad commercial-kitchen equipment portfolios used by restaurants and foodservice operators. The underfollowed lane is thinner but includes Farmer Brothers as a micro-cap speculative exception with explicit coffee-equipment servicing exposure, and Westrock Coffee as a small-cap B2B beverage-solutions supplier to foodservice/restaurant customers where equipment/service exposure still needs verification. Expanded the restaurant equipment/service node into a two-lane universe. The strongest direct public-market anchor is Middleby, a commercial foodservice equipment manufacturer with restaurant and institutional kitchen exposure. The underfollowed lane is thinner because several highly relevant service networks and parts distributors are private or recently taken private; Farmer Brothers was a strong beverage-equipment service candidate but appears to have closed a take-private transaction in May 2026, so it is retained as a coverage-gap/comparable rather than a US-listed candidate. Public small/mid-cap candidates with plausible second-order exposure include Westrock Coffee as a beverage-solutions platform for restaurant/foodservice customers and Distribution Solutions Group as a speculative MRO/supply-chain-services proxy that still needs restaurant-customer proof. Layer 1B expanded the restaurant equipment/service node into a two-lane universe.
